column5: forgetting the God who brought Israel out
column6: After warning Israel to beware when full and settled, Moses says not to forget YHWH who brought them from Egypt; remembered rescue corrects self-sufficiency and grounds response to instruction.

column5: forgetting amid prosperity
column6: Israel is warned not to forget YHWH by failing to keep his commands when prosperous, a concrete case where a hearer's inner memory determines whether the received teaching governs life.

column5: claiming power for oneself
column6: The imagined heart says its own power made its wealth; this is a specific counterpart to the commentary's self-sufficient hearer who sees no lack and therefore has no reason to seek what was lost.

column5: fear expressed in walking, love, and service
column6: Moses asks what YHWH requires and lists fearing him, walking his ways, loving and serving him, and keeping his commands; fear is an inward posture that issues in a whole course of action.

column5: fear known through costly obedience
column6: The angel says Abraham's fear of God is now known because he did not withhold his son; fear is disclosed by a concrete response, not a group identity or mere claim.

column5: fearing YHWH while walking without light
column6: Isaiah describes the person who fears YHWH, obeys the servant's voice, and walks in darkness without light yet trusts God's name; this concretely joins fear, hearing, and trust before visible resolution.

column5: YHWH himself as the one to fear
column6: Isaiah redirects fear toward the holy Lord of hosts; it supplies an explicit object for the commentary's deliberately uncompleted “whoever fears” and frames awe as response to the transcendent.

column5: the Creator's boundary for the sea
column6: The sea's fixed limit is given as evidence of YHWH's power, followed by the question whether people will fear him; the created order grounds the reverence that the surah's opening creation signs also invite.

column5: failure to say in the heart, “let us fear”
column6: Despite seasonal rain and harvest, the people do not say in their hearts that they should fear YHWH; this locates the missing response inwardly even when signs are present.

column5: remembering God's works across generations
column6: The purpose of teaching the next generation is that they set hope in God, do not forget his works, and keep his commands; this joins transmitted reminder, recovered memory, and action.

column5: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
column6: The commentary labels Arabic ذ ك ر; Psalm 78 uses Hebrew זכר when it says Israel did not remember God's hand or the day he redeemed them, a concrete use of the cognate for lost rescue-history.

column5: forgetting the hand that redeemed
column6: Israel fails to remember a deliverance it experienced and therefore repeats distrust; this adds the commentary's point that forgetting can be a failure to pursue what was once known.

column5: children summoned to learn fear
column6: The speaker calls children to listen and promises to teach them the fear of YHWH, making reverence a learned response to instruction rather than an inherited label.

column5: hearers who tremble at the word under pressure
column6: Isaiah addresses those who tremble at YHWH's word even as their own brothers cast them out; the verse shows reception of the word persisting when the surrounding community rejects them.

column5: seeking YHWH with trembling in the latter days
column6: In the latter days Israel will seek YHWH and David their king and come trembling to YHWH and his goodness; fear is a movement toward seeking, not mere flight.

column5: hearing today without hardening the heart
column6: The quotation warns its hearers that when they hear God's voice they must not harden their hearts; the immediate, personal response to a reminder is the point.

column5: the heard message failing to benefit
column6: The wilderness generation heard good news but it did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith; this makes the commentary's distinction between a reminder passing across and being taken in explicit.

column5: reminder of rescue followed by destruction
column6: Jude says he wants to remind readers who already know that the Lord saved a people from Egypt and later destroyed the unbelieving; memory of rescue becomes a warning about the response that follows.

column5: remember, repent, and do the first works
column6: The church is told to remember its former state, repent, and do its first works, with removal of its lampstand threatened if it does not; recollection must become action while there is time.

column5: remembering what was received and heard
column6: The church is told to remember what it received and heard, keep it, and repent, or the coming will be unexpected; this directly joins received speech, memory, vigilance, and a deadline.

column5: remembering endurance after illumination
column6: Readers are told to remember earlier days after they were enlightened, when they endured public suffering; recollection strengthens present fidelity rather than serving as passive recall.

column5: Peter remembers after denying Jesus
column6: After Peter denies Jesus, the Lord's look makes him remember the prediction, and he weeps bitterly; this gives a precise, painful case of a warning remembered only after failure.

column5: mercy to those who fear God through generations
column6: Mary says God's mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation, carrying the commentary's individual inner quality across time without making it an ethnic class.

column5: past events written as warnings for readers
column6: Paul says Israel's events were written as warnings for those at the end of the ages; this makes scriptural memory a present admonition with consequences, like the commentary's reminder before judgment.

column5: command to remember the risen Christ
column6: Paul directly commands Timothy to remember Jesus Christ raised from the dead; the verse gives a concrete Christian instance of remembered proclamation as the hearer's continuing task.

column5: remembering Jesus' words after the resurrection
column6: After Jesus is raised, the disciples remember his saying about the temple and believe; the delay shows how an event can restore the meaning of a word previously heard.

column5: Moses trembling at Sinai
column6: Hebrews recalls that even Moses said he trembled with fear at the terrifying manifestation; it supplies a concrete bodily response to divine presence alongside the later call to worship with reverent awe.

column5: not sharing opponents' fear
column6: Peter tells believers not to fear what their opponents fear or be troubled; this distinguishes reverence toward God from social intimidation, a useful limit on the commentary's broad language of fear.

column5: honoring Christ as holy in the heart
column6: The next verse directs believers to honor Christ as Lord in their hearts; with 1 Peter 3:14, it specifies where fear and reverence are directed when human pressure is present.

column5: fear following visible judgment
column6: After Ananias and Sapphira die, great fear comes upon the church and all who hear; this is a counter-sequence to fear before sight, showing fear arising after a judgment has become visible.

column5: heart closed against hearing and turning
column6: Jesus cites people whose heart is dull and whose ears and eyes are closed lest they understand, turn, and be healed; this gives a specific account of refusal at the level of perception that blocks a reminder's effect.

column5: service without fear after deliverance
column6: Zechariah speaks of being rescued from enemies so that God's people may serve him without fear; the context makes this freedom from human threat, not the reverent fear of God in the commentary, a meaningful distinction.

column5: fear of the Lord as wisdom's beginning
column6: Ben Sira calls fear of the Lord the beginning of wisdom and associates it with the faithful; this places reverence at the start of understanding, complementing the commentary's link between knowing and fear.

column5: those fearing the Lord wait for mercy
column6: Ben Sira tells those who fear the Lord to wait for his mercy and not turn aside; fear sustains a listener through delay rather than being only an immediate fright.

column5: fear of God taught as communal conduct
column6: Clement urges the community to fear the Lord and to teach the young fear of God; this concretely extends the commentary's personal reception of reminder into instruction and conduct across a community.
